comments.body:
Thanks @patschi, great report, you found a real bug. At some point the Scheduler page in the old admin saved a Disabled entry for the backup job into `user/config/scheduler.yaml`, and that entry overrode the Scheduled Backup switch, which is why turning it off and on did nothing. The proc_open notice is unrelated, it only affects the Run buttons.

The next release fixes it: the switch on the Scheduler page and Scheduled Backup on the backup profile are now the same setting, and old entries are ignored and cleaned up. Until then, removing the `default-site-backup` line under `status:` in `user/config/scheduler.yaml` gets your backups running again.

Thanks, appreciated!

An idea: The "Run" button could force a job run the next time the cron runs, instead just disabling it.

title: [Feature]: hermes cron cancel — on-demand termination of a live in-flight cron run
body:
# [Feature]: `hermes cron cancel JOB_ID` — on-demand termination of a live in-flight cron run

## Problem

There is no way to cancel a live, in-flight cron run from the CLI or from the cronjob management tool. If a scheduled job wedges (e.g. a no-agent script job that hangs on network I/O or a stuck child process), the only recourse is to wait out the scheduler's own timeout or perform manual process-group forensics with `kill`.

## What happened (incident, verified 2026-10-04)

A nightly no-agent script job (a bash wrapper running a CLI subprocess) wedged and stayed hung for ~53 minutes. Investigation into the running system found:

- `hermes cron --help` lists verbs `list / create / add / edit / pause / resume / run / remove / rm / delete / status / runs / history / incidents / notepad / doctor / tick` — there is **no cancel / abort / stop verb**.
- `hermes cron pause JOB_ID` only prevents *future* fires. It does nothing to a run already in flight.
- The job runs as a real subprocess tree (bash wrapper → child processes) in its own process group under the gateway PID, so it *is* killable — but only manually, after using `ps`/`pgrep` to discover the process-group ID and issuing `kill -TERM -<pgid>`.
- A gateway restart does not clear it either: the restart drain does not auto-exclude long-running script jobs within its wedge allowance (observed 48h).
- The scheduler's own timeout (`HERMES_CRON_TIMEOUT`, default 3600s) eventually SIGTERMs the process group — but that is a 1-hour wait. In this incident the job timed out as an incident on consecutive nights before being manually killed (`exit code -15`).

## Current options and why each is insufficient

| Option | Why it's insufficient |
|---|---|
| Wait for `HERMES_CRON_TIMEOUT` (default 3600s) | Up to a 1-hour hang per occurrence; noisy timeout incidents; the wedge can repeat nightly before anyone intervenes. |
| Manual `ps`/`pgrep` + `kill -TERM -<pgid>` | Works, but requires root-cause forensics on a live gateway, is error-prone (wrong pgid kills an unrelated job), and is not scriptable or safe for non-operators. |
| `hermes cron pause JOB_ID` | Only suppresses *future* fires; a run already in flight is untouched. |
| Gateway restart | The restart drain does not auto-exclude long-running script jobs within its wedge allowance, so a restart doesn't clear the run. |

## Prior art (maintainers already invest in this area)

- #18004 — timeout marks a job failed while the worker thread keeps running
- #39782 — containment + same-job non-overlap on timeout
- #62014 — run-claim heartbeat + liveness guard before stale one-shot removal
- #63406 / #64365 — prevent long-running scheduled scripts from running twice

None of these add an on-demand cancel of a live run.

## Proposal

Add a `hermes cron cancel JOB_ID` verb (plus an equivalent cancel action in the cronjob management tool) that:

1. Looks up the run's tracked process group for the currently in-flight execution.
2. Sends `SIGTERM` to the process group.
3. Escalates to `SIGKILL` after a short grace period if the group hasn't exited.
4. Records the run with a `cancelled` status (and a corresponding incident), so `hermes cron runs`/`history` stays truthful about what happened.

This should be explicitly distinct from the existing verbs:

- **`pause`** — prevents future fires only; does not touch a live run.
- **`remove`/`delete`** — deletes the schedule; not a targeted "stop this run now" action.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `hermes cron cancel JOB_ID` terminates a currently running execution of that job.
- [ ] Cancel works for **script jobs** (real subprocess trees, killed via process group) and for **agent jobs** (the equivalent of interrupt + containment, per the semantics introduced in #39782).
- [ ] `SIGTERM` first, with escalation to `SIGKILL` after a short grace period.
- [ ] The job remains scheduled for its next fire after a cancel — cancel is per-run, not per-schedule.
- [ ] `hermes cron runs`/`history` shows the run

comments.body:

- The agent path has the same seam: `_abort_if_fire_claim_lost()` runs from the run watcher and does `agent.interrupt(...)` when `cancel_event.is_set()`, so a cancel signal that reaches the run interrupts a live agent turn too.

Both existing producers live inside the gateway process and neither is an operator surface: fire-claim loss, and the dashboard drain transport. `hermes_cli/subcommands/cron.py` registers list/create/edit/pause/resume/run/remove/status/runs/incidents/notepad/doctor/tick and nothing else, and `tools/cronjob_tools.py` has no `cancel` occurrence at all.

The 404s were mine and they were mechanical, not a GitHub-side path problem: I was POSTing `head` as the bare branch name, and for a fork the field has to be qualified as `kokhlo:<branch>`. Bare `fix/...` validates against the base repo's refs, where that branch does not exist, so GitHub rejected it before it ever got to the cross-repo path — it just reports as "head invalid" (422), which is easy to misread as a permissions wall. A scheduled job (`mnemosyne-nightly-sleep.sh` + its `mnemosyne sleep --all-sessions` child) hung mid-run and held up the gateway's Telegram lane. There was no on-demand cancel, so termination meant an operator-assisted kill outside the scheduler: SIGTERM to the job's process group — deliberately the same TERM mechanism the scheduler's own timeout path uses, so the job took its normal failure path and was recorded failed rather than falsely successful. Exactly the capability requested here, exercised by hand because it doesn't exist yet.

A second observation both occurrences of this class share: the drain report makes target identification harder than it should be — it displayed the gateway's own pid (46494) attributed as the job's (`external`), so finding the actual process tree to kill required manual inspection. title: f4-424-pro TOS 7.0 docker netcloud, paperless sync workaround
body:
My first post, I am not any type of programer. Started a home lab and was getting this up and running to my tnas, internal only until i figure out how it all works and if it can replace my one-drive and gdrive for music, photo, video, and documents. Below is the workaroud I had to complete. 

f4-424-pro TOS 7.0 with all of the latest updates
Paperless-ngx Version 3.3.3, Install Type docker, Server OS Linux-6.12.63+-x86_64-with-glibc2.41, Database Type postgresql, Redis
Nextcloud Hub 26 Summer (35.0.2),PostgreSQL 15.19 on x86_64-pc-linux-musl, compiled by gcc (Alpine 15.2.0) 15.2.0, 64-bit, Paperless Sync set to use cron, Paperless Unified Search

when I run 
docker exec -u www-data nextcloud_app php cron.php 
nextcloud will update with the new files in paperless-ngx. 
General setting are set to use cron but cron in the sync app does not work. 
paperless sync would just be stuck in the Queued synchronization status.


To verify the correct path to cron.php inside your nextcloud_app container, you can use a few simple Docker commands to inspect the file structure.
Here is how you can check and verify the exact path:

1. Search for cron.php inside the container
Run this command to search the container for the file and print its exact path:
Bash
docker exec -u www-data nextcloud_app find / -name cron.php 2>/dev/null
What to look for in the output:
Whatever path it outputs is the absolute path you should use.

2. Check the container's working directory
You can also check what directory the container lands in by default:
Bash
docker exec -u www-data nextcloud_app pwd
If it outputs /var/www/html, then running just php cron.php works because you are already in the folder containing the file.
the TOS 7's task scheduler strictly forces a 1-hour minimum.
you can easily spawn a lightweight background loop script on your NAS that fires every 5 minutes without touching the core crontab file manually.
Create a simple shell script on your NAS (e.g., at /Volume1/public/paperless/nextcloud_cron.sh):
Bash
#!/bin/bash
while true; do
    docker exec -u www-data nextcloud_app php -f /var/www/html/cron.php > /dev/null 2>&1
    sleep 300
done
Make it executable:
Bash
chmod +x /Volume1/public/paperless/nextcloud_cron.sh
You can then use the TOS 7 Scheduled Tasks wizard to run this script on system startup (or once a day)
and the loop will handle firing your docker exec command every 300 seconds (5 minutes) continuously in the background!

For the paperless consume folder. 
create the share using tnas control pannel> file share. 
set group perms to read and write for my groups.
then set these permmisions and restarted the container.
chown -R 0:0 /Volume1/paperless_inbox
chmod -R 775 /Volume1/paperless_inbox
chmod g+s /Volume1/paperless_inbox

If so, that's a completely different project, which runs directly inside Nextcloud and **PULLs the data from Paperless using the Nextcloud's background job scheduler**.

My project, on the other hand, is a Docker container as part of the Paperless stack that **uses WebDAV to synchronize data using a PUSH machanism**. It has its own filesystem watcher and does not depend on Nextcloud's cron system, which is why my project provides instant syncronisation without relevant delay (takes 2-10 sec).

title: Issue: PHP cron jobs produce output but do not execute side effects
body:
I've noticed a strange issue with PHP CLI commands executed through cron.

When I run a command such as `php8.x test.php` from a cron job, the script appears to run and produces the expected output, but the actual operations don't seem to happen.

For example, I have a PHP script that deletes or clears the Redis cache. When executed through cron, the command prints the expected output, but the Redis cache remains unchanged. If I run the exact same command manually from a terminal (for example, the VS Code terminal), it produces the same output **and the operation is performed successfully**.

This makes it look as though the cron job is executing the script but not completing its actual operations, even though there are no obvious errors in the output.

Could this be caused by a restriction in the cron sandbox, a difference in the PHP CLI environment, or some limitation involving Redis access or permissions?

Since the same command works correctly in the terminal, it would be helpful to understand why its behaviour differs when executed through cron.

Could you investigate whether cron jobs run with a different environment or sandbox configuration that might prevent PHP scripts from performing these operations, and suggest how to diagnose the issue?

Thank you!

comments.body:
Thanks for the clear report. Cron runs a site's PHP inside the same sandbox as that user's SSH login: the user's own home, a read-only system, and only the sockets the panel passes in. A terminal opened as root isn't sandboxed at all.

Until #2108 (the fix for your #2059), that sandbox didn't include the Redis socket, so a script run from cron couldn't reach Redis. I reproduced it on a test server: a PHP cron job printed all its normal output and finished, while its Redis call failed with "No such file or directory". With #2108, the same cron job wrote to Redis. #2108 is merged; it reaches the development channel with its next build and stable on November 1.

To see which case you're in, add this line to the script, or run it as its own cron job, and read the output in the cron job's log:

```php
var_dump(file_exists('/run/redis/redis.sock'));
```

`false` from cron means your server doesn't have #2108 yet. If it prints `true` and the cache still isn't cleared, please paste the error your Redis client throws (catch it and echo `$e->getMessage()`), and say whether the terminal where it works is root or the site's user.

Thanks for the update. I’m on the development channel, so I already have the latest changes, including #2108 and #2123, but the issue still persists.

When I run the cron job from the panel as the hosting user, the behaviour has changed after #2123. Previously, the job displayed the page’s output, including output from statements such as die(), but the actual operations performed by the script had no effect. For example, the Redis cache was not cleared.

After #2123, the cron job no longer displays the script’s output. Instead, the panel only reports Exit code 0 and marks the execution as successful. However, the actual operation still does not happen, and the Redis cache remains unchanged.

Running the exact same PHP CLI command from the VS Code terminal works correctly: it produces the expected output and the operation is performed. Redis also works from the CLI now, as the previous connection error is gone.

So, it seems that #2108 fixed Redis socket access, and #2123 changed how cron output is handled, but neither has resolved the underlying issue I’m experiencing: the script appears to exit successfully when executed through the panel’s cron system, yet its intended side effects do not occur.

Could you investigate whether the cron runner is actually executing the script correctly, whether it is using the expected PHP binary and working directory, and whether any sandbox restrictions or error-handling changes could be hiding a runtime failure?

Thank you.

Thanks, the script made this reproducible. Two separate things are going on. **Why the cache isn't cleared** The site's Redis credential (`t_`) isn't allowed to run `SCAN`. It can only reach keys under its own `jt::` prefix, and `SCAN` walks the whole keyspace. phpredis doesn't throw when Redis refuses it, and your loop's exit and failure checks both read the refused call as "no more keys". So the function collects nothing, deletes nothing and returns `true`. I ran your function on a test server with a site's credential and one key under its prefix. It printed `Flush cache in progress...
Cache flushed successfully.`, the key was still there afterwards, and `$cache->getLastError()` held: ``` NOPERM this user has no permissions to run the 'scan' command ``` The result was the same through cron's Run now and when run directly as the site user outside the cron sandbox, so cron isn't what makes the difference. That means the terminal run isn't using the same connection. Either it authenticates as a different Redis user, or it reaches a different Redis server (a VS Code terminal can be running on your own machine rather than the server). Could you tell us how `$cache` is built (socket or host, and which username), and whether the VS Code terminal is a session on the server, and as which user? Adding `var_dump($cache->getLastError());` right after `flushRedisCache($cache);` will show it: from cron it prints the `NOPERM` line above. To clear the cache from cron,

Thanks for the detailed explanation. I think I understand the issue now, and I'll modify my code accordingly.

I don't need to flush Redis through the API, as I'm already aware that this is possible with `curl`. My use case is a little different: I have certain pages and operations that need to run through cron, and in those cases, I need to clear the entire Redis cache as part of the PHP script itself.

I'll adjust the implementation to work within the permissions available to the site's Redis user, rather than relying on `SCAN` across the entire keyspace.

Thanks again for investigating and clarifying what's happening.

I'm not sure what changed, but I've been experiencing this issue since yesterday. The PHP script runs perfectly when I execute the exact same command manually from the terminal, but when I run it through the panel's cron system, it doesn't behave as expected. To clarify, **this issue is not related to Redis**. The script I'm testing has nothing to do with Redis; I'm experiencing the same problem with other PHP scripts as well. When I execute the command through cron, the execution modal doesn't display the script's output. The logs aren't helpful either, as they only show the command ID and its name, without any actual output, errors, or details about what happened during execution. Since the same command works perfectly in the terminal, I suspect there may be an issue with how the panel executes cron jobs, captures their output, or handles the execution environment. Could you investigate why PHP scripts behave differently when executed through cron compared to running the exact same commands manually from the terminal? It would also be helpful if the execution modal and logs exposed stdout, stderr, and any relevant errors to make troubleshooting possible.

Thanks, that was the missing piece. I could reproduce it, and it isn't your script.

**Why Run now shows no output and the log is empty**

Run now and the job's log read the job's output from the system journal, as your account. That only works when the server keeps the journal on disk. journald gives each account its own journal file, which that account can read, only in that case.

If the journal is kept in memory (`Storage=volatile`, or `Storage=auto` without a `/var/log/journal` folder), your account can't read it. Run now then reports "Exit code 0" with no output, and the log stays empty, although the job did run. On a test server with a volatile journal I got exactly your screenshot, while the file the test job writes was written.

This is fixed on main (#2143), and the development channel picks it up with its next update. The panel now reads the job's output itself, limited to your account's lines. Run now shows stdout and stderr, PHP warnings and fatal errors included, and the log shows each run.

To check that it's the same cause on your server, run `ls -ld /var/log/journal`. "No such file or directory" means the journal is volatile.

**Why a script can work in the terminal but not from cron**

A cron job runs in your home directory (`/home/<you>`), not in the folder of the script. When you type `php8.3 test2.php` inside the script's folder, relative paths resolve against that folder. From cron they resolve against your home.

A script that reads or writes `cache/…`,

The cron execution modal still doesn’t display the script’s output, and the execution logs remain empty or don’t contain any useful information.

I also checked whether the server uses persistent journald storage, as suggested:

root@panou:~# ls -ld /var/log/journal
drwxr-sr-x+ 4 root systemd-journal 4096 Oct  4 12:38 /var/log/journal

The /var/log/journal directory exists, so this doesn’t appear to be the volatile journal scenario described in your explanation.

One important detail: until a few updates ago, the cron execution modal displayed the script’s output correctly. This behaviour changed after a recent update, so it seems possible that a regression was introduced in the cron output handling or retrieval mechanism.

title: HIGH: the first cron call after every process start is refused as lock-held because acquireLock fails closed during the Redis handshake
body:
Two behaviours compose into a silent missed job:

1. `refuseIfCronLockHeld(key, ttl)` (by design) **acquires** the lock as its check and does
   not release it — `ttlSeconds` is also the minimum spacing between accepted runs.
2. `lib/cache/acquireLock` fails **closed** while `redis.status !== 'ready'`.

`web` is the process that serves the cron routes, and the first request after a start races
its own Redis handshake. The result is a `423`/skip that is indistinguishable from a
legitimate concurrent run, and — because the failure is a returned lock object rather than a
thrown error — it is not logged as anything. On this host the nightly `backup` job was
skipped this way after every `pm2 reload`. The workaround is that the second call always
succeeds, which is exactly the kind of "it works when I try it manually" that hides a
scheduler that never fires.

Fail-closed on the lock is the right security default; doing nothing about it is not.
Options, cheapest first:

- `await once(redis, 'ready')` with a short timeout before the first `acquireLock`.
- Keep fail-closed, but emit a distinct reason (`lock-unavailable` vs `lock-held`) so the
  operator can tell "Redis is still connecting" from "another run owns it". `recordCronSkip`
  already writes a `logError` row for refusals — the same hook can carry the distinction.
- Add a Prometheus counter for cron skips by reason, and alert if `backup` skips at its
  scheduled time. A missed nightly is currently only discoverable by noticing that the
  nightly is missing.

title: [Bug]: Dokploy Cloud application schedule runs manually but never executes automatically
body: ### To Reproduce 1. Use Dokploy Cloud v0.30.0 with an application deployed to an active remote server. 2. Open the application's Scheduled Tasks section. 3. Create and enable an application schedule with: - Cron: `*/5 * * * *` - Timezone: UTC - Shell: `sh` - Command: `bun run cron:stripe-topup-reconcile` 4. Wait for several scheduled intervals. 5. Observe that no automatic execution or deployment-history entry is created. 6. Trigger the same schedule manually. 7. Observe that the manual execution completes successfully. 8. Disable and re-enable the schedule, then save it again. 9. Change the cron expression to `* * * * *` and wait for several minutes. 10. Observe that automatic execution still never occurs. Other scheduled tasks attached to the same application and remote server execute automatically. ### Current vs. Expected behavior ### Current behavior The schedule record is saved correctly and reports `enabled: true`. Its cron expression and application association are also correct. Manual execution works and produces a successful deployment record in approximately five seconds. Automatic execution creates no deployment record at all. This also occurs with `* * * * *`, so it is not specific to the five-minute expression. ### Expected behavior An enabled application schedule should be registered with the Dokploy Cloud scheduler and execute according to its cron expression. Each execution should create a deployment-history entry. ### Provide environment information ```bash Operating System: Control plane: Dokploy Cloud Remote server OS: Ubuntu 24.04.3 LTS Arch: Kernel: 6.8.0-100-generic (x86_64) Dokploy version: v0.30.0 VPS Provider: Hetzner Application/service: Bun/TypeScript backend running in a Docker container Schedule type: Application Deployment target: Remote server ``` ### Which area(s) are affected? (Select all that apply) Application ### Are you deploying the applications where Dokploy is installed or on a remote server? Remote server ### Additional context Dokploy API inspection confirms that the schedule is persisted with: - `enabled: true` - `scheduleType: application` - the expected application association - the exact submitted cron expression - UTC as the default timezone The deployment history contains only manually triggered executions. Other schedules attached to the same application execute automatically, which rules out a stopped application, unavailable remote server, or globally broken scheduler. A Sentry Cron monitor independently reports every expected execution as missed. Possible source-level lead: in the current Dokploy source, the Cloud paths in `schedule.create` and `schedule.update` invoke the asynchronous `schedule(...)` registration function without awaiting it: https://github.com/Dokploy/dokploy/blob/canary/apps/dokploy/server/api/routers/schedule.ts That function performs the request to the Cloud jobs service: https://github.com/Dokploy/dokploy/blob/canary/apps/dokploy/server/utils/backup.ts If registration fails or does not finish, the schedule database update can still succeed without surfacing the scheduler-registration failure. ### Will you send a PR to fix it? No

title: bug(maintenance): an unready ServicePrincipal reports MaintenanceReady=True, and the CronJob outlives it
body:
## What

Two facets of one code path in the Catalog controller (`crates/stardelt-operator/src/maintenance.rs`, the `match principals.get_opt(&principal)` at ~line 423):

1. **Existence is treated as readiness.** `Some(_)` immediately writes `MaintenanceReady=True reason=Scheduled` and applies the CronJob, without reading `status.ready`. A `ServicePrincipal` that exists but was never provisioned (Secret `sp-<name>` missing, `Ready=False reason=ClientNotSetUp`) therefore reports a maintenance schedule that can never run.
2. **The CronJob outlives the principal.** The `None` branch only sets `NoRunner`; it never deletes the CronJob it created earlier, so the job keeps firing against a principal that is gone.

## Why it matters

The Catalog condition is the only signal an operator has that table maintenance runs. Built this way it can say `True Scheduled` while every nightly run dies at container start (`secretKeyRef sp-<name>` is `optional: false`), and no condition says so.

## Observed (dev cluster, chart install, 2026-11-11)

After applying a `ServicePrincipal pipeline-stardelt-admins` (owner `stardelt-admins`) on a chart install, where no `PlatformInstance{identity.mode: platform}` exists so the operator never creates the Keycloak client (see `principal.rs:205-214`):

```console
$ kubectl -n stardelt get serviceprincipal pipeline-stardelt-admins -o jsonpath='{.status.ready} {.status.conditions[0].reason}'
false ClientNotSetUp
$ kubectl -n stardelt get catalogs -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{" "}{range .status.conditions[?(@.type=="MaintenanceReady")]}{.status}{" "}{.reason}{"\n"}{end}{end}' | grep -E 'shared|warehouse'
shared True Scheduled
warehouse True Scheduled
$ kubectl -n stardelt get secret sp-pipeline-stardelt-admins
Error from server (NotFound): secrets "sp-pipeline-stardelt-admins" not found
$ kubectl -n stardelt get cronjob maint-shared -o jsonpath='{.spec.jobTemplate.spec.template.spec.containers[0].env[?(@.name=="PIPELINE_CLIENT_SECRET")].valueFrom.secretKeyRef}'
{"key":"client-secret","name":"sp-pipeline-stardelt-admins","optional":false}
```

And after deleting the `ServicePrincipal` again (5+ minutes, two 300 s cycles):

```console
$ kubectl -n stardelt get catalogs ... | grep -E 'shared|warehouse'
shared False NoRunner
warehouse False NoRunner
$ kubectl -n stardelt get cronjobs -o name | grep -E 'maint-shared|maint-warehouse'
cronjob.batch/maint-shared
cronjob.batch/maint-warehouse
```

The two CronJobs were then deleted by hand to restore the cluster to its previous state.

## Suggested change

- Split the `Some(_)` arm on `status.ready`: ready -> `True Scheduled` + apply (today's behaviour); present but unready -> a distinct reason (for example `RunnerNotReady`) carrying the principal's own message, and no CronJob.
- In the `None` arm, delete the CronJob (and its Jobs) that this catalog's controller created.
- A unit test per arm, next to the existing pure tests around `cron_job` / `merge_condition`.

Found while working stardelt/stardelt-platform#1026 (the seed's maintenance principal); this behaviour is why that ticket's premise looked plausible.


---

## Ready to implement — architect, verified 2026-11-12T00:25Z

`v0.4`, `P1`. A verified patch: apply it with `git apply`, run the verify below, open a PR. The
whole change is 2 files and one test module; nothing else in the operator moves.

### The patch

Apply on a fresh branch from `origin/main` (`7d05d7b`). Save it as `583.patch` and run
`git apply 583.patch`.

```diff
diff --git a/crates/stardelt-operator/src/controller.rs b/crates/stardelt-operator/src/controller.rs
index 1e60f28..a7453d1 100644
--- a/crates/stardelt-operator/src/controller.rs
+++ b/crates/stardelt-operator/src/controller.rs
@@ -754,7 +754,10 @@ async fn remove_lakehouse_finalizer(ctx: &Context, lh: &Lakehouse) -> Result<(),
 /// Delete a named object, treating `404` as success. A `Delete` is not atomic:
 /// after a partial run the next reconcile starts from the top,

title: feat: CronJob demo-reset — empty the public demo's playground at 03:00 UTC (public demo D)
body:
## Why
The public demo's playground (epic stardelt/stardelt-platform#895, decision 4) is written to by anyone on the internet. Every night at 03:00 UTC it must be emptied and get its one schema `scratch` back. This needs no IdP admin and no new credential:
- the job signs in as the existing principal `pipeline-demo` (group `demo` owns `playground`);
- it talks only to the query engine.

**Land after #896.**

## The trust anchor (why this ticket is longer than it looks)
`trinoUrl` in ConfigMap `stardelt-identity` is the **TLS** endpoint `https://trino.<ns>.svc.cluster.local:8443` (`scripts/identity-bootstrap.sh:173`), signed by the namespace CA in Secret `trino-ca` (`manifests/trino-tls.yaml`, key `tls.crt`). Plain HTTP is refused. The token endpoint is the **public** issuer (`https://id.alpha.dev.stardelt.io/realms/stardelt`), so the job needs two trust stores, not one:

- the public WebPKI roots for OIDC discovery and the token request (the `python:3.13.16-slim-bookworm` image carries `ca-certificates`; `manifests/access-sync.yaml`'s `wait-for-idp` already proves it on this cluster);
- exactly one extra anchor, Secret `trino-ca` key `tls.crt`, for the Trino requests — the same invariant Nova (`NOVA_TRINO_CA_PEM`), Airflow and JupyterHub follow. Do not disable verification and do not set `SSL_CERT_FILE` globally: that would replace the public roots.

default trust store: failed: URLError <urlopen error [SSL: CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED] certificate verify failed: self-signed certificate in certificate chain (_ssl.c:1032)>

title: fix(maintenance): the table list includes the engine's system schema — every catalog's run reports a failure
body:
# fix(maintenance): the table list includes the engine's `system` schema — every catalog's run reports a failure

## Milestone and priority

`v0.4`, `P2`. Cause confirmed on the live cluster 2026-11-10 02:0xZ (the first nightly run of
operator#476's CronJobs); the fix is one SQL predicate.

## What happens

The maintenance CronJob `maint-mobility` (the operator's `stardelt maintenance run --catalog
mobility`, image `ghcr.io/stardelt/stardelt-cli:dev`) logged this first line and exited 1:

```console
$ kubectl -n stardelt logs job/maint-mobility-29904600
{"table": "system.iceberg_tables", "smallFiles": 0, "optimized": false, "seconds": 0.371, "error": "TrinoUserError(type=USER_ERROR, name=TABLE_NOT_FOUND, message=\"line 1:22: Table 'mobility.system.\"iceberg_tables$files\"' does not exist\", query_id=20261110_020050_00012_wzcyc)"}
…
{"catalog": "mobility", "tablesDone": 4, "tablesFailed": 9}
```

Every catalog's run reports at least this one failure, so every job exits 1 and
`status.maintenance` says a run failed even when every real table succeeded.

## Cause

`stardelt/maintenance.py`, `_tables(catalog)`:

```python
return (
    f"SELECT table_schema, table_name FROM {stardelt._quote_ident(catalog)}.information_schema.tables "
    "WHERE table_type = 'BASE TABLE' AND table_schema <> 'information_schema'"
)
```

A Trino Iceberg catalog lists its `system` schema (`iceberg_tables`, `iceberg_files`, …) as
`BASE TABLE` in `information_schema.tables`. The loop then treats `system.iceberg_tables` like a
data table and asks for `"system"."iceberg_tables$files"`, which does not exist.

## Steps

### 1. `stardelt/maintenance.py` — leave the engine schema out of the list

In `_tables(catalog)`, extend the predicate (keep the two-line form):

```python
def _tables(catalog):
    """The catalog's base tables as ``(schema, table)``, engine schemas left out."""
    return (
        f"SELECT table_schema, table_name FROM {stardelt._quote_ident(catalog)}.information_schema.tables "
        "WHERE table_type = 'BASE TABLE' "
        "AND table_schema NOT IN ('information_schema', 'system')"
    )
```

Nothing else changes: `run()` already skips `excludeTables` and records one line per table.

### 2. `tests/test_maintenance.py` — pin the predicate

`FakeConnection.answer` compares against `maintenance._tables("warehouse")`, so it keeps working.
Add one test next to the other `_tables` assertions:

```python
def test_the_engine_schemas_are_not_maintained():
    sql = maintenance._tables("warehouse")
    assert "'information_schema'" in sql
    assert "'system'" in sql
```

## Verify

```console
$ python -m pytest tests -q
… passed

$ python -c "from stardelt import maintenance; print(maintenance._tables('mobility'))"
SELECT table_schema, table_name FROM "mobility".information_schema.tables WHERE table_type = 'BASE TABLE' AND table_schema NOT IN ('information_schema', 'system')
```

CI runs `python -m pytest tests -q` (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`).

## After merge

The job runs the CLI image, not the checkout: `ghcr.io/stardelt/stardelt-cli:dev` must be rebuilt
(python's image workflow) and the operator's pinned digest (`operator#482`) bumped in a follow-up
ticket — the same pattern as `NOVA_IMAGE`. Do not bump it in this PR.

## Open questions

None.

title: roles/cron never starts the cron daemon when the package is already installed — backups are written and silently never run
body:
`roles/cron` never starts the cron daemon on a host that already has the package — backups then silently never run

## The code

`deploy/ansible/roles/cron/tasks/main.yml` (as of #2611):

```yaml
- name: Check whether crontab is already installed
  ansible.builtin.command: sh -c 'command -v crontab'
  register: cron_crontab_present
  changed_when: false
  failed_when: false

- name: Install cron
  ansible.builtin.apt: { name: cron, state: present, ... }
  when: cron_crontab_present.rc != 0

- name: Ensure the cron daemon is enabled and running
  ansible.builtin.service: { name: cron, state: started, enabled: true }
  when: cron_crontab_present.rc != 0          # <-- here
```

The task whose whole job is "the daemon is enabled and running" runs **only when `crontab`
was absent**. On a host where the `cron` package is present but the service is stopped,
masked or not enabled, the role checks, finds `crontab`, skips both remaining tasks and
reports success. Nothing ever starts cron.

## Why it matters more than its size

The role's own header says it is "the scheduler every `ansible.builtin.cron` task in this
repo writes to". Those tasks are (10 of them, across 6 files, verified on #2611's head):

- `playbooks/backup.yml` — **2 tasks: the backups themselves**
- `roles/backup-monitor` — the thing that would notice backups failing
- `roles/llamenos-maintenance` — 4 tasks
- `roles/alerting`, `roles/geoip`, `roles/llamenos-ntp-monitor` — 1 each

So the failure mode is: `ansible-playbook` succeeds, every cron job is written to the
crontab correctly, and **none of them ever fires** — including the backups and including
the monitor that exists to notice. For a crisis hotline that is a silent data-loss path, and
it is invisible precisely because the deploy reports green. This is the
"[defences must be visible](https://github.com/Llamenos-Hotline/llamenos-platform/issues/1495)"
rule: a scheduler that is not running must not look the same as one that is.

The condition is reachable without anyone doing anything exotic — a trimmed base image, an
image where cron ships disabled, or a host where someone stopped it once.

## The fix

Drop the `when:` from the enable/start task. `ansible.builtin.service` with
`state: started, enabled: true` is idempotent and a no-op on a host where cron is already
running, so the guard buys nothing and costs the only case it was meant to cover. The
`Install cron` task's `when:` is fine to keep — that one genuinely only needs to run when
the package is missing (and it is what keeps the role privilege-free on a host that already
has it, per the header comment).

Worth checking while in there: whether `state: started` alone is enough if the unit is
**masked**, and whether a smoke-check should assert the daemon is active after a deploy
rather than trusting the role — the preflight/smoke-check playbooks already exist and an
assertion there is what would make this visible instead of silent.

## Provenance

Not a regression — #2611 introduced the role and carried this shape from the start, and
`fleet/review` flagged it as a non-verdict-changing note on that PR. Filed separately rather
than grown into #2611, which is scoped to its own three guards.

title: Project users' crontabs survive the kill loop and removal
body:
## Problem

A project user's crontab survives the kill loop and the removal that #297 builds (security review round 1 on #441, finding F1). In a session the user runs `crontab -` with a per-minute job. The kill loop finds no process, boots out `user/<uid>` and answers clean, and the removal answers removed. A minute later root `cron` starts `/bin/sh -c` as that UID, for the VM's lifetime, during other projects' sessions. `pwpolicy -disableuser` and the `/usr/bin/false` shell don't stop it, because cron doesn't authenticate the user.

This goes against S13-01-process-hardening ("No process is meant to keep running after its project leaves the VM's effective policy") and SEC08-proj-isolation. It is not exploitable on main today, because nothing starts a process as a project user yet. It must hold before project-user sessions ship (#303, #304).

Checked read-only on a macOS host: `/usr/sbin/cron` links no PAM, `/usr/lib/cron/cron.deny` names only `Guest`, and `/usr/bin/crontab` is setuid root. Not reproduced in a guest.

## Proposed fix (from the review)

- In the image, write `/usr/lib/cron/cron.allow` with `root` only, so a project user can't register a crontab, and check that `at` is denied too.
- In the kill loop, before the first signal of each round, unlink `/private/var/at/tabs/<name>` as root, so an existing tab goes with the first kill.
- Update S13-01 (or S13-02 "Known gaps") to name cron and `at` as schedulers that the image and the kill loop close.

## Done when

On a macOS guest, a project user's `crontab -` is refused, and a tab placed by hand is gone after `KillUser`, with no process of that UID started afterwards. Needs a VM.

Co-Authored-By: lsimons-bot <bot@leosimons.com>
Assisted-by: Claude:claude-opus-5-5

- Where the lock is enforced: the image build is V1-M7 and isn't built yet, so an image-only `cron.allow` would leave the gap open until then. `wb-guestd` enforces it at each start, before it creates or unlocks any project user: it writes `/private/var/at/cron.allow` and `/private/var/at/at.allow` with `root` only (`/usr/lib/cron` is a symbolic link to `../../var/at`, which is on the writable data volume, not the sealed system volume). If either write fails, it fails closed and logs the rule. The image recipe gets the same two files when V1-M7 builds it.

title: ui-server: a transient module discovery failure at cron start silently drops every module job until the next restart
body:
## Context

`brain-ui-cron crontab` adds module jobs only when module discovery succeeds at the moment the cron service starts. If discovery returns nothing usable, the crontab silently gets only the core jobs, and stays that way until the next container start:

- `readModuleList` returns `null` for a non-zero exit, empty stdout or an unparseable payload, without writing anything to stderr (`packages/ui-server/src/bin/brain-ui-cron.ts:160-188`).
- When the host is not `reconciled`, discovery is skipped and `modules` is `null`, also silently (`brain-ui-cron.ts:223`).
- Only a thrown error reaches the `module discovery unavailable` stderr line (`brain-ui-cron.ts:226`).
- `emitCrontab` then writes the comment `# (brain module list unavailable — module cron skipped)` (`packages/ui-server/src/cron/emit.ts:175`). Nothing retries, nothing appears in Activity, and the job's last failure just stops recurring.

Observed on a hosted 0.44.0 install: after one container start the crontab carried only the core jobs and that comment, and the supervisor's cron error log was empty. Run by hand an hour later as the same uid, through the same maintenance worker, `brain-ui-cron crontab` emitted the module job correctly. So discovery failed transiently at boot, most likely while app or native readiness was still settling, and a scheduled module job (`odysseus-beacon-run` in the Odysseus example) stopped running without any signal.

## Scope

- Report why discovery yielded nothing: exit code, the stderr tail, or "host not reconciled".
- Retry discovery a bounded number of times before falling back to core jobs only.
- Make "module jobs skipped" visible to the operator, for example a status/Activity entry or a failure notification, not only a crontab comment.

## Out of scope

- The module job execution boundary itself.
- Re-running discovery periodically after boot. Note it as an option only.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A test with a discovery that fails once and then succeeds produces a crontab containing the module job.
- [ ] A test with persistent failure writes a stderr line naming the cause, and records an operator-visible "module cron skipped" state.
- [ ] The existing byte layout of a successful crontab is unchanged.

## Verification

Unit tests over `emitCrontab` and the `crontab` subcommand with a stubbed boundary; no live host.

## Contract impact

None beyond operator diagnostics.

comments.body: Triaged: ready to work. The acceptance criteria, scope and verification are checkable, and no ruling is needed. Set to p1 under the blocker-priority rule, because silently dropping every module job breaks a scheduled nightly job. Milestone 0.45.0.

Claiming (claim token `wi-3381-6fdbc75a`). Branch: `fix/3381-cron-discovery-retry` from `origin/main` @ f8284d6cc. Collision report for the cited files: closure-only (#3056, #3059, #3069, #3116, #3292, #3293), no direct path collision. Staying out of #3380's scope.

title: Refresh run publishes its provenance, so a post-release check needs no ssh
body:
After a release, the only way to confirm which code the itri refresh ran was to ssh in and read the HEAD and the log. Agents get that ssh denied as "Production Reads", so Matt ran it by hand. The public snapshot age shows that refresh is running, but not which code ran.

Fix: have the refresh run write its git SHA, its run start and end, and its outcome into `snapshot/<MAC>.context.json` (or a small `snapshot/<MAC>.status.json`). Then a post-release check is a curl of the public site. Do not change the dashboard contract, or if it must change, bump SCHEMA_VERSION per CLAUDE.md.

Also record the exact refresh crontab line in `docs/agents/operations.md` as the single source, and drop the catchup and keep-alive history from its crontab line. The panel filed #244 because that line was not in the repo.

From the release-threads retro, 2026-11-02.

title: Move the inbox sync from crontab to a systemd timer and alert when it goes stale
body:
## Problem

`scripts/inbox_sync.sh` (Dropbox vault -> local inbox, every 5 minutes) is the one recurring Genesis job still scheduled from the user crontab instead of a systemd user timer, and nothing watches whether it is still running.

On a live install the crontab entry disappeared (a local test run of an unshimmed `uninstall.sh` path removed it; see PR #3006). The cron daemon kept running, the inbox monitor kept scanning, and every health surface stayed green, while no new inbox source note reached the install for 5 days. The only evidence was the age of the last entry in `logs/inbox_sync.log`.

## Proposed change

1. Move the sync to a systemd user timer + oneshot service rendered from a template like the other `genesis-*` units (`OnCalendar=*:0/5`, `Persistent=true`), so it is enumerated by `systemctl --user list-units 'genesis-*'`, survives crontab edits, and is enabled/disabled by the same install and uninstall paths as every other unit. Keep the script's existing `flock` single-flight.
2. Add a freshness signal: the health/watchdog layer reports the inbox sync as degraded when the last successful cycle (`--- done ---` marker, or a small state file the script writes on success) is older than a threshold (e.g. 30 minutes), and alerts through the normal health-alert path. Installs that do not configure an inbox vault report "not configured", not degraded.
3. Update `uninstall.sh` to disable the timer instead of filtering crontab lines, and keep the crontab cleanup only as a migration step for old installs.

## Acceptance

- `systemctl --user list-timers` shows the inbox sync timer on an install with a configured vault.
- Removing or stopping the timer produces a health alert within the threshold.
- Tests for the new unit template and freshness check never touch the real crontab or real systemd (shimmed).

comments.body:
**Second failure mode, observed on the same install: the first sync after an outage deletes every response written during it.**

Step 2 of `scripts/inbox_sync.sh` treats "local `.genesis.md` older than 10 minutes and absent from a healthy vault listing" as a user deletion. The script's own comment records the gap ("a response whose push never landed … is reaped after the grace period", deferred). During a multi-day sync outage the monitor keeps writing responses that are never pushed, so the first healthy cycle afterwards removes all of them: here, 15 response files in one cycle, with only the bulk-cleanup WARNING line as a trace. They were recoverable from the evaluating sessions' transcripts (rebuilt byte-identically, verified against surviving files), but nothing in the script makes that possible by design.

This should be fixed together with the timer move, since the timer move alone does not prevent it:

1. A durable "seen on the vault" ledger: record each response filename the first time it appears in a healthy vault listing (or after a successful push). Only a file that was once seen on the vault and is now absent counts as a user deletion. A never-pushed file is pushed, never reaped.
2. Until that exists, refuse to reap when the bulk threshold trips (more than 5 in a cycle) and log loudly instead. A deliberate mass deletion in the vault is rare and can be finished by hand; an accidental mass reap loses work.
3. Inbox responses are not covered by `scripts/backup.sh`; c

**It recurred.** On the same live install, the user crontab was found completely empty again on 2026-10-28. The last `inbox_sync.log` cycle was 2026-10-11 01:50Z, about a day after the restore that followed the first gap. Nothing alerted for 17 days. The cause of the second wipe was not established: the only crontab writer in the repo is `uninstall.sh`, and its tests now shim `crontab`. That recurrence is the case for doing this issue rather than re-adding the line by hand.

**A restore hazard worth encoding in the fix:** `inbox_sync.sh` runs its cleanup (step 2) before its push (step 3). After an outage, every response written locally during the gap is older than the 10-minute grace and absent from the vault, so the first cycle after a plain restore deletes all of them as "user deletions" (see #2804). Recovery on this install was done in three steps:

1. Push exactly the gap's responses first: `rclone copy` with `--files-from` set to local-minus-vault, restricted to files newer than the last good cycle so nothing the user deleted is resurrected.
2. Check that the remaining local-minus-vault set is empty.
3. Only then restore the schedule.

A timer-based fix should either make the script safe after a gap (a presence record, per #2804) or make the staleness alert say "do not simply restart" until that lands.

title: imps: start dispatching at logon/boot (at-logon trigger on imps-dispatch, @reboot cron)
body:
Set-and-forget goal: a machine that boots (or a user who logs in) starts dispatching on its own, without waiting up to an hour for the `:07` slot.

## Today
- `imps/setup.ps1` registers `imps-dispatch` with `schtasks /SC HOURLY` only (plus the 5-min `imps-label-watch` when enabled). No logon/startup trigger.
- `imps/setup.sh` writes `7 * * * * $HOURLY` (plus `*/5` label-watch) to crontab. No `@reboot` entry.

## Wanted
1. **Windows:** add an **at-logon trigger with a ~2 min delay** to the *existing* `imps-dispatch` task (not a second task). `warlock.mjs` checks "exactly one dispatch task" by counting tasks whose action runs `hourly.cmd`, so a separate `imps-dispatch-boot` task would trip it. At-logon (not at-startup) because the runner needs the user profile (`~/.claude/settings.json`, `gh` auth). If adding the trigger fails (policy/elevation), warn and keep the hourly task: never fatal.
2. **Unix:** add `@reboot sleep 120 && $HOURLY` to the crontab block. The existing `grep -vF "$HOURLY"` dedupe and `uninstall.sh` already remove any line containing `$HOURLY`, so re-running setup stays idempotent.
3. Overlap is safe: `dispatch.lock` makes a boot-time cycle and the hourly/label-watch ticks mutually exclusive.

## Related
- #63 (systemd user timer when crontab is absent): if that lands, its timer should get `OnBootSec=2min` too.
- The 9router-wait issue (filed alongside): at boot 9router may not be up yet, so this pairs with the router backoff.

title: [Bug]: Isolated cron message send intermittently fails with "Cron receipt authority is unavailable" (2026.10.6)
body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

An ordinary isolated `agentTurn` cron run on stock OpenClaw 2026.10.6 completed its collection step but its official `message` tool call failed with `Cron receipt authority is unavailable; wait for Gateway settlement or restart.`, leaving the scheduled notification unconfirmed.

### Steps to reproduce

NOT_ENOUGH_INFO

### Expected behavior

For a still-active, unchanged authorized occurrence, a supported message consumer should coordinate any necessary preparation/settlement before initiating one external effect. A genuinely revoked/cancelled/expired occurrence or unconfirmed writer outcome must still fail closed; an uncertain external send must not be blindly retried.

The stock asynchronous `acquireUse()` path queues behind the writer in the isolated control. I am **not** asking to remove the synchronous guard: stock owner tests explicitly expect `readForPreparation()` to reject while a writer is pending.

### Actual behavior

Sanitized observed timeline, timestamps normalized to UTC:

```text
2026-10-25 01:00:00  existing scheduled run starts
2026-10-25 01:00:42  official tool_call -> core message returns:
  Cron receipt authority is unavailable; wait for Gateway settlement or restart.
2026-10-25 01:00:53  agent ends with an explicit incomplete-delivery result;
  no confirmed sent/messageId/settled receipt was returned to this attempt
```

Collection and message construction had completed. This was about 53 seconds into a 600-second run, not an execution-timeout incident. Physical external delivery for this failed attempt remains unconfirmed; absence of a receipt is not asserted as proof of no external effect.

A different native-script job reached the QQ transport later before the Gateway was restarted, and the operator received that message. This is only a channel-availability control at another time/path, not proof that the failed attempt succeeded or that native scripts are immune.

### OpenClaw version

2026.10.6 (`fe06181`), stock installed runtime. No core patch was applied for the incident or the investigation.

### Operating system

Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS, Linux x64; Node.js v24.22.1.

### Install method

npm-global package layout; Gateway managed by a systemd user service.

### Model

`stepfun/step-5-preview`, as recorded by the failed run.

### Provider / routing chain

NOT_ENOUGH_INFO

### Additional provider/model setup details

Recorded provider identifier: `stepfun`; API: `openai-completions`; intermediate routing is not supplied. The model returned a valid tool call; the error arose at the host's official message invocation. No provider overload or model idle/execution timeout was observed for this failure. Provider/model causality is not established.

### Logs

Only the error and normalized timestamps above are supplied. Raw prompts, destinations, message content, account/job/run/session identifiers, private filesystem paths, endpoints, database rows and credentials are intentionally excluded.

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

#### Observed workflow / reproduction limits

There is no deterministic full-Gateway reproducer for the production failure yet. The observed workflow was an existing time-based isolated `agentTurn`, with `toolsAllow: [read, exec, message]`, a 600-second timeout, `lightContext: true`, and `delivery.mode: none`. It collected current data, constructed a normal plain-text `message` send through the deferred core tool, and received the error below. It stopped without replaying the uncertain send. No stream schedule or shutdown was requested during that observed run.

title: T05: Background jobs with Procrastinate
body:
**Project:** artysci-dla-szkol

**Model:** sonnet

Depends on: #64

**Story:** US-0.6

**Goal:** a reliable job queue on Postgres for generation, e-mail and media work.

**In scope**
- Procrastinate with the Django integration: one queue per kind (`default`, `ai`, `media`, `email`), retries with backoff, idempotency keys, a periodic task scaffold (cron-like) for reminders and cleanups.
- `make worker` (native) and the `worker` service in Compose `full`.
- A `jobs` admin page (read-only list of recent jobs and failures) for the admin panel later.
- A demo job `ping` that writes a row, used by tests and by T09's smoke check.

**Out of scope:** actual AI/e-mail/media jobs (their own tasks).

**Acceptance criteria**
- Given the worker running, when `ping` is deferred, then it runs within 5 s and its row exists.
- Given a job that fails twice and then succeeds, then it is retried with backoff and ends `succeeded`.
- Given the same idempotency key deferred twice, then the job runs once.

**Tests:** the three criteria, using Procrastinate's test connector or a real Postgres in CI.

**Verification:** on pirx, defer `ping` and show the worker log line.

**Definition of done:** the shared DoD for M0 (ruff, pytest ≥85% on new code, migrations checked, no secrets, env-only config, docs updated, CI green, approved and merged by the AI reviewer).

title: Bug: cron scheduler – failed command in prompt job recorded as success
body:
## Problem
A prompt cron that tells the agent to run a shell command is recorded as `success: true` even when that command fails. The cron health view shows the job as healthy, so nobody notices.

Seen on a peer node: a nightly `wiki absorb` prompt cron pointed at a release directory that had been pruned. The command failed with `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` on 4 nights in a row, and every run record said `success: true`. A second prompt cron failed the same way.

## Cause
`src/crons/scheduler.ts:619`, in the prompt-job path, sets `success: !response.error`. That only reflects whether the agent run itself errored. The agent ran, reported the failure in its text, and the run counted as a success. Command jobs (`executeCommandJob`, line ~479) use the exit code and are not affected.

## Expected
A prompt job whose instruction is "run this command" should be recorded as failed when the command exits non-zero, so `agentx_crons` shows it as failing and `onError` fires.

## Possible fixes (for the implementer to choose)
1. Let prompt crons declare a check (e.g. `expectExitZero` / require an `EXIT=0` marker in the response) and mark the run failed when it is missing.
2. Or document that shell work must use `command:` jobs, and warn at config load when a prompt matches `^Run(:| this shell command)` with a CLI path.
3. Either way: at load, warn when a cron prompt or command names a path that does not exist.

## Acceptance
- [ ] A test where the prompt cron's command fails records `success: false` and counts as failing in cron health.
- [ ] Existing prompt crons whose agent run succeeds and that have no command check are unchanged.

## Summary

A run performs one revision round and ends. The publish job already knows whether the round left work outstanding (`result.json`: `review.verdict`, `checks.state`, `mergeable`), and the report already derives lists from those results, yet nothing starts the next round: the hourly scan does, hours later, or a person dispatches by hand. Add a `continue` job to the cron caller that re-dispatches this workflow for the pull requests whose round ended with work outstanding, so the Copilot review cycle runs unattended until the review is clean, the pull request is handed off, or a cap is reached.

## Evidence

`lfreleng-actions/gha-workflow-linter#466` (issue #465), 2026-11-10: five rounds in 1 h 50 min, each dispatched by a person two to three minutes after the previous verdict (runs 42868904108, 42874337449, 42878183592, 42882466635, 42885453659, 42888647013); then a 🟡 review at 20:05 and nothing until the 06:00 slot. `docs/DESIGN.md` §2 keeps "acting on a review in the same run" a non-goal, and that stands: the next round is a **new run** with a fresh select job that re-reads everything from GitHub, a fresh session, and the same trusted publish. title: Add recurring scheduled runs that start a one-shot bravebot run from a cron expression
body:
A person cannot ask bravebot to run a prompt every weekday morning. /loop and schedule_next live inside one open session and end with it, so a recurring job (a dependency check, a summary of merged pull requests) needs a cron entry the person writes and maintains by hand. Cline stores named schedules, keeps them across restarts and shows a history of each run.

## What Cline does

`cline schedule create "name" --cron "expression" --prompt "task" --workspace /path` makes a schedule from a five-field cron expression. Schedules persist across process restarts and run independently of any terminal session. At each trigger time a new session is created and the agent is run. The `cline schedule` wizard lists schedules, previews upcoming runs, pauses and resumes, triggers one immediately, shows execution history with duration, tokens and cost, and deletes. Results can be routed through connectors such as Telegram. Available in the SDK, CLI and Kanban, and it needs the local hub process running.

> Scheduled agents persist across process restarts and run independently of any terminal session.

Sources:

- <https://docs.cline.bot/cli/scheduling.md>
- <https://docs.cline.bot/sdk/guides/scheduled-agents.md>

## What bravebot does today

Nothing stores a schedule. /loop and schedule_next repeat a prompt or ask a turn to run again inside one running session, and end when the session ends. A one-shot `-p` run exists and can be started from the operating system's own scheduler, but bravebot does not write that entry, list it or show what its runs cost.

Read: `docs/specs/loop.md LOOP-1`, `docs/specs/tools/schedule-next.md SCHED-1`, `docs/specs/cli.md CLI-1`, `docs/specs/sessions.md SESSION-11`

## Proposal

Add a `bravebot schedule` subcommand (add, list, remove, run-now, history). An entry is written by a person at the command line and holds a cron expression, a prompt, a directory and optional flags, stored in the state directory. It is installed as an operating-system scheduler job (crontab, launchd or a systemd timer) that runs the existing one-shot `-p` path, so no bravebot daemon is needed and the layering spec is unchanged. The prompt is the person's own text and is fixed when the entry is written, as LOOP-1 fixes a loop's line; nothing a run reads can edit it or add an entry. Each run is an ordinary recorded session, so `history` is a list of those with the cost SESSION-11 already records. A new spec clause would say that a scheduled run is a one-shot run and is approved as CLI-1 approves one. The tests: a run started by the job writes nothing a one-shot run would refuse, an entry cannot be created from inside a turn, and a run's record is listed by `history`.

## Constraints

CLI-1 says an allow rule decides nothing for an unwatched run, so a scheduled run can read and report but can write only when the entry carries --dangerously-skip-permissions, which the person types when creating the entry (MODE-5). The design has to state that limit in `list` output. A notifier for the result overlaps the open issue about hook moments that call a person back. Sending results to a chat service is the connector gap, not this one.

## Where this comes from

The `peer-features` skill compared the Cline documentation with what other coding agents publish, at `9f14c42a3bf4`. A second pass checked that each source says what is claimed, that bravebot lacks it and that it fits the specs. Filed by a tool rather than a person, so no `importance`, `urgency` or `size` has been judged.

Gap id: `parity-scheduled-agents`

title: [Enhancement] Workflow Runs: lifecycle states (scheduled/in-progress/done/cancelled) + schedule types, implemented in code
body:
## Parent

Sub-issue of Qunsultant/cfagent#2786 (Workflow Runs). Part 3 of #2786 merges Docs-tab
columns into Workflow Runs; this slice makes the Workflow Runs page a true workflow
lifecycle surface: every workflow shows where it is in its life, how it was scheduled,
and why that schedule type was used — and the schedule types we do not use yet get
implemented, not just surveyed.

## Requirement (implementation in code, not research)

The Workflow Runs page (`?tab=workflow-runs`) must surface, for every workflow run:

1. **Lifecycle state — exactly one of: scheduled, in-progress, done, cancelled.**
   - The page's current status vocabulary is richer than these four
     (`queued`, `running`, `held`, `awaiting`, `completed`, `partial`, `failed`,
     `skipped`, `cancelled` in `src/services/workflowRuns.ts`). The slice defines
     the mapping from every existing status onto the four states, pins it in tests,
     and guarantees no run is left unclassified and no run drops off the page
     because of the new state. The four states are filterable and sortable at
     Docs parity (see #2786 Part 2 columns).
   - `scheduled` covers runs that are scheduled but have not fired yet — they must
     appear as scheduled rows, not as absences. `cancelled` covers runs cancelled
     via scheduler cancel / workflow terminate — they must appear as cancelled
     rows, never vanish.
2. **Schedule type per run, plus why that type.**
   - Every run carries its scheduling mechanism, its schedule identity (cron
     expression, schedule id, or delay), and the reason that mechanism was chosen.
     The reason is recorded at schedule-creation time and surfaced on the run —
     not a document-only rationale.
   - The page gains a schedule-type filter alongside Trigger/Status/Reports.
3. **The missing schedule types, implemented.**
   - Reference: the "schedules" tab of the shared doc
     (https://docs.google.com/document/d/1WaoyhH5vVTRO1Sf7gWu8IMmUptcvkJoEDaFiBcl9NIA/edit?tab=t.31xfk3fa699x)
     lists five Cloudflare scheduling mechanisms. Grounded against main
     (2026-11-03, tip f14f3f88):
     - USED: Cron Triggers (3 wrangler crons: token renewal, ScheduledAgent tick,
       retention/research, all routed through `scheduled()`); Cloudflare Queues
       (SCREENER_EVENTS + SCREENER_EVENTS_DELIVERY with DLQs, stage pub/sub);
       Agent Scheduler (port in `src/actors/actorPorts.ts`, adapter in
       `src/actors/cfAgentsAdapter.ts`, live caller in `src/agents/nlq/execution.ts`).
     - NOT USED: Workflow Schedules (cron attached to a workflow binding — none of
       the four bindings in wrangler.jsonc carries a `schedules` field); direct
       Durable Object alarms (zero `setAlarm`/`alarm()` uses in `src/`).
   - The slice implements, as working code with runs visible on the page:
     - (a) at least one workflow moved onto binding schedules, replacing its
       current cron-to-`scheduled()`-to-dispatch path for that firing;
     - (b) agent-scheduler schedules (including the existing NLQ ones) surfaced as
       runs with their schedule identity, so a scheduled NLQ task is visible
       before it fires and as done/cancelled after;
     - (c) delayed-queue work surfaced with its delay, distinct from immediate
       stage events.
   - Each newly implemented mechanism ships with at least one live-visible run
     per mechanism on the page (scheduled state before firing, terminal state
     after) — a mechanism with no visible run does not count as implemented.

## Acceptance

- Every existing run status maps to exactly one of the four lifecycle states;
  the mapping is pinned by tests and every run on the page shows a state.
- Every run shows mechanism + schedule identity + reason; the schedule-type
  filter works across families (screener, saga, payment, trading, NLQ).
- At least one run per newly implemented mechanism is visible on the page in
  both its scheduled and terminal states (or cancelled, where a cancel is
  exercised).
- No

title: Identity hard constraint `NEVER write memory records` denies cron capture recovery, but a turn's own terminal capture writes the candidate with no policy check
body:
## Summary

An agent's identity profile has the hard constraint `NEVER write memory records`. The constraint is loaded into the agent's `SecurityPolicyEngine`. An unmodified SDK turn then runs. Its terminal capture writes the extracted memory candidate: `memory_capture_state: succeeded`, disposition `succeeded`, one output id. The security policy is not asked about that write.

For the same capture, two gates in the same runtime say no:
- the recovery gate that the cron executor passes to capture recovery (`memory_capture_recovery_allowed`) returns `False`;
- the turn's own tool-policy adapter does not allow the `memory.write` tool.

Both answer `require_approval` with `identity_hard_constraint_restricted`. The results are the same on the published 0.1.13 and on `dev` @ `68d623d1`.

This is the first note from my 0.1.13 verification of #420. As you asked when you closed #420, I am filing it on its own, with an unmodified successful write and the loaded constraint. It has no fix proposal. Nothing is injected in this reproduction.

## Minimal reproduction

The relevant keys of the config file (written with `save_config`; paths shortened):

```json

  "default_agent": "openminion",
  "agents": {"openminion": {"provider": "openai", "default_channel": "console"}},
  "providers": {"openai": {"api_key_env": "PROBE_420_PROVIDER_KEY", "base_url": "http://127.0.0.1:<port>/v1"}},
  "runtime": {"process_mode": "single-process", "daemon_auto_start": false},
  "storage": {"path": "<root>/.openminion/state.db"},

}
```

`<root>/identity/openminion/profile.yaml`:

The `openai` base URL points at a scripted OpenAI-compatible server on 127.0.0.1. It answers the auto fact extraction with one `user_preference` item (`user_preference:indentation`).

Steps:

2. Write the config and the profile above.

       tool_name="memory.write", tool_spec=port.tools.get("memory.write"), args={})

The same on 0.1.13 and `dev`.

- `profile.yaml` is under the configured `identity.bundle_root`.
- `IdentityCtl.get_profile("openminion").role.hard_constraints` is `["NEVER write memory records"]`.

- The provider gets 4 requests: the auto fact extraction, `decide` and 2 freshness checks.

Confirmed independently with your inspected probe against installed OpenMinion 0.1.13: all 9 observation checks passed. With the loaded `NEVER write memory records` identity constraint, an ordinary SDK turn wrote the capture candidate/receipt/result without a memory-write policy evaluation. The recovery check and bound memory.write policy adapter denied the same agent afterward; the neutral identity control allowed both. The provider was a local scripted HTTP server, not a live model. title: job apply: a launchd backend on macOS, so scheduled Claude jobs keep the keychain login and its claude.ai connectors
body:
## Problem

#141 / #142 made `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` (from `claude setup-token`) the standard way to run scheduled Claude jobs on macOS, because cron cannot reach the login keychain. That works, but **a setup-token run has no claude.ai connectors**. For any runbook whose data lives behind a connector (Metabase, Gmail, Slack, …), the token path is not a fix.

Measured with the same prompt ("list your `mcp__claude_ai_*` tools"):

| How the job was started | Login | Connectors | Wall time |
|---|---|---|---|
| crontab line (`job apply`) | keychain unavailable → `Not logged in` | — | fails in ~4 s |
| crontab line + `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` | token | **none** (`NO_CLAUDE_AI_MCP`) | ok |
| LaunchAgent in `gui/<uid>` (`launchctl bootstrap`) | keychain login (`security show-keychain-info` succeeds) | **all of them** (e.g. 21 Metabase tools) | ok, 10 s end to end |
| terminal / `env -i` from a terminal | keychain login | all | ok |

Environment: macOS 27.0.1, Claude Code 2.1.317, aits `c37df30dd6ad`. The launchd hangs and slowdowns cited in #141 (#99760, #95689 upstream) did not reproduce here, but this was one run, not a soak.

So on macOS, launchd is the only scheduler that gives an unattended `claude -p` the same capabilities as a terminal.

## Proposal: a launchd backend for `job apply` on macOS

Keep the jobs file as the single source of truth and let `job apply` install each job as a LaunchAgent instead of a crontab line. Either make it the macOS default for jobs, or select it per file or per job (`"scheduler": "launchd"`).

- One plist per job: `~/Library/LaunchAgents/<prefix>.<name>.plist`.
  - `ProgramArguments` is the same `aits job run NAME --timeout … --on-alert … -- COMMAND` the crontab line runs today. Locking, logs, alerts and `job list` stay unchanged.
  - `EnvironmentVariables.PATH` comes from the file's `path`.
- `schedule` becomes `StartCalendarInterval`. Lists expand to one dict per combination; ranges and steps expand the same way. A schedule that would expand to too many entries is refused with exit 2, the same as other invalid input.
- Install with `launchctl bootstrap gui/<uid>`, remove with `launchctl bootout`. Owning the `<prefix>.*` plists gives the same ownership model as today's crontab block: `added`/`changed`/`removed`/`unchanged`, and it refuses a plist it did not write.
- Side benefit: launchd runs a calendar job missed while the Mac slept once on wake. Cron silently skips it.
- Documented limit: a LaunchAgent runs only while the user is logged in to the GUI. That is fine for a desktop that stays logged in, but not for a headless box, where the token path from #142 remains the answer.

This stays within "aits never stays in the background; the OS scheduler owns the schedule". It swaps which OS scheduler gets the job; it does not add an aits daemon.

## What we run meanwhile

A ~120-line script that reads the same jobs-file schema and writes and bootstraps one LaunchAgent per job, as described above. Our run scripts use the keychain login when `security show-keychain-info` succeeds, and fall back to `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` only when it fails. We would rather delete the script than maintain it, which is why we are asking for this in aits.

Related: #141 (cron / keychain), #142 (token pass-through).

The measurements here show what we need: on macOS, only a process in `gui/<uid>` keeps both the keychain login and the claude.ai connectors. Rather than translate every job into its own LaunchAgent, we propose that aits run the schedule itself, in one foreground process that a single LaunchAgent supervises. #145 drops P15's out-of-scope list, which named a resident scheduler; P10 already allows a looping command the user starts in the foreground and supervises.

| State | spread across launchctl and N plists | one process, one jobs file |
| Missed runs after sleep | whatever launchd does | a rule aits defines and documents |
| Install | bootstrap or bootout per job | one LaunchAgent (`KeepAlive`), or one systemd user service |

- `aits job sched FILE` reads the same jobs file as `job apply`, with the same `path`, `env` and `hosts` handling. It runs in the foreground until it gets a signal.

## Production evidence (Nov 3, 2026, CST)
Roll displays the cover and correct mapping for **Hellblazer #3, "Going For It"**, ComicVine **issue 29319**, but no creator section. UI reads **"Creator credits queued for fetch…"** even though ComicVine's issue page shows creators.

Read-only production Neon evidence, branch `br-silent-violet-ayobfez5`, captured around **2026-11-04 03:54 UTC**:
- `external_identities`: ComicVine issue `29319`, identity `23445`, has `creator_credits: []`, no `raw_provider_payload.person_credits`, no `deep_metadata_refreshed_at`.
- `comicvine_metadata_refresh_requests` for that identity: `state=pending`, `attempts=0`, `last_error=NULL`, created/updated **2026-11-04 03:50:00.866 UTC**.
- Backlog by state: **21 pending, all 0 attempts; 24 running, all with expired leases; 13 completed**. Some running requests reached **76 attempts**, indicating repeat claims without durable completion.

Vercel production function logs (deployment `dpl_71Xz8ev3JhPMRkXucWnD2yHZu368`) at **03:53:20–03:53:50 UTC** repeatedly report `comicvine_metadata_repair_drain_failed`. Stack: `_drop_finished_drain -> drain_due_metadata_repairs -> _drain -> refresh_repository.claim_due_requests -> db.execute -> asyncpg.connect`; underlying `asyncio.exceptions.CancelledError` during asyncpg TLS/connect. These are on GET `/api/v1/issues/1119581/comicvine` responses, not on scheduled cron. This is consistent with the detached background task being cancelled after the serverless HTTP response.

## Root cause
The fix for #4148 added a **durable request ledger** but kept execution opportunistically in a per-request detached `asyncio.create_task` (`schedule_metadata_repair_drain`). Durable bookkeeping is **not durable execution**. The Vercel Python runtime cancels work while fetching a DB connection, before a pending issue is even claimed. Retried GETs just schedule more work that can be cancelled. The daily recovery cron in `vercel.json` runs at **10:00 UTC once a day** and drains **at most 10 requests** per invocation; this cannot promptly clear 45 already-due active requests, even assuming it executes successfully.

Relevant code:
- `app/services/comicvine_intelligence.py`: persists repair request, commits, calls `schedule_metadata_repair_drain()`.
- `app/services/comicvine_metadata_repair.py`: detached task via `asyncio.create_task`; claim/lease/retry implementation.
- `app/api/cron.py` and `vercel.json`: daily capped recovery path.
- `frontend/src/pages/RollPage/components/ComicIdentity.tsx`: polls `refresh_pending`, but can never surface credits until a worker persists them.

## Required fix
1. Make actual repair execution **durable and timely within existing free infrastructure**. A request may enqueue but must not depend on an unawaited serverless `asyncio.create_task`. Preserve the confirmed ComicVine mapping, issue ownership, ratings, reading progress, and roll responsiveness; no paid provider or unrequested staging/shadow mode.
2. Reconcile already-pending and expired-running rows; bound batch size, concurrency, provider pacing, connection usage, retries, and terminal states. Ensure repeated GETs and multi-instance concurrency cannot create a claim storm. Verify the daily cron actually runs successfully and that its cadence/capacity are adequate, without assuming the next day's cron can clear arbitrary backlog.

Include serverless task cancellation before DB checkout, expired lease recovery, provider throttling/absence, and legitimate `person_credits: []`.
4. Production proof on the same issue identity: `attempts>0`, terminal `completed` and nonempty normalized creator credits (if provider supplies them); check backlog starts decreasing and task cancellation is no longer the execution mechanism. Only then close the issue.

title: Desktop-launched gateway has minimal PATH after update; AIM MCP servers and script crons fail (aim: not found)
body:
## Summary

After a Toolbox auto-update of Kiro Crew, the gateway started by the desktop app has a minimal `PATH` (`/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin`). Every stdio MCP server or script cron that depends on a user-installed binary now fails. A script cron that had posted to Slack through `slack-mcp` every weekday stopped working with no config change on the user's side.

## Impact

- A weekday script cron (`ctx.call_tool("slack-mcp", "post_message", ...)`) posted on Nov 3, 4, 5 and 6. It has failed on every run since.
- The failure only shows up as a dashboard-bell notification, so the user's team got no report and nothing visible said the job was broken.
- `gh` called through `subprocess` from the same cron failed first with `[Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'gh'`. That one was worked around by hard-coding `/opt/homebrew/bin/gh` in the script.

## Error

```
Slack post failed: MCP server 'slack-mcp' disconnected during 'initialize' (rc=127);
stderr tail: ~/.aim/mcp-servers/slack-mcp: line 2: exec: aim: not found
```

`~/.aim/mcp-servers/slack-mcp` is the standard AIM wrapper:

```sh
#!/bin/sh
exec aim mcp start-server slack-mcp "$@"
```

`aim` lives in `~/.toolbox/bin`, which isn't on the gateway's PATH. `~/.kiro/settings/mcp.json` launches the server by bare name (`"command": "slack-mcp"`), and that's the default AIM setup.

## Timeline

| When | Event |
|---|---|
| Nov 6 11:01 | Last successful scheduled Slack post |
| Nov 6 11:22 | Toolbox installed Kiro Crew 0.12.0.9 |
| Nov 7 onward | Gateway restarts from the desktop app; the cron fails every run (`gh` not found, then `aim: not found`) |
| Nov 11 23:57 | Toolbox installed 0.12.1.2; the gateway process still runs with `PATH=/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin` |

Gateway process (`ps eww`):
```
PATH=/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin
.../KiroCrewInternal/runtime.noindex/0.12.1.2/KiroCrew.app/Contents/Resources/backend-dist/...
```

## Expected

The gateway, MCP servers and script crons run with the user's login-shell PATH, or at least with `~/.toolbox/bin`, `/opt/homebrew/bin` and `/usr/local/bin` added. Then AIM-installed MCP servers and common CLIs resolve the same way they do when the gateway is started from a terminal (`kirocrew restart`). An update shouldn't silently change this.

## Suggestions

1. When the desktop app launches the gateway, resolve the user's login-shell environment, or append the well-known tool directories above to PATH.
2. When a stdio MCP server exits with `rc=127` (command not found), say which binary was missing and show the PATH that was used.
